title: What can a bitcoin: link ask a wallet to do?
dek: A bitcoin: link carries an address, an amount and other ways to pay, in a form any wallet can open. BIP 321 says which parts a wallet must understand and which it may ignore.

blocks.text: Click a payment link on a web page, or scan a QR code, and a wallet opens with the payment filled in. Both carry the same thing: a `bitcoin:` URI. It is a request, not a payment: a wallet MUST NOT act on it without the user's approval.

BIP 21 defined the scheme in 2012. BIP 321 replaces it and describes how links are used now: several ways to pay in one link, keys in any letter case, and room for new payment methods that older wallets can safely skip.

figure.title: One link, read by three wallets
figure.caption: Choose one of BIP 321's example links. The model cuts it into parts, decodes the values, and reads it as three illustrative wallets would, each implementing different keys. The example addresses are intentionally invalid.

blocks.text: A link is `bitcoin:`, an address, and optional parameters after a question mark, joined by ampersands. The address may be a base58 P2SH or P2PKH address, a bech32 or bech32m SegWit address, or nothing at all.

`amount` is in decimal BTC, with a period and no commas: `amount=50.00` and `amount=50` both mean 50 BTC. `label` names the recipient and `message` describes the payment. Characters outside the allowed set are encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded, so a space becomes `%20`.

blocks.title: A payment link, part by part
blocks.caption: BIP 321's 50 BTC example, one part to a row. The model percent-decodes its message.

blocks.text: The scheme and the parameter keys are case-insensitive, while values and addresses can be case-sensitive. BIP 21 had made the keys case-sensitive, but QR codes mostly use uppercase, so reading keys in any case was already common.

blocks.title: Lowercase and uppercase
blocks.caption: The same two SegWit addresses as a lowercase and an uppercase link, both from BIP 321's examples. With case-insensitive keys, both give the same payment instructions.

sections.heading: More than one way to pay

blocks.text: Parameters can carry other ways to pay: `lightning` for a BOLT 11 invoice, `lno` for a BOLT 12 offer, `pay` for BIP 351 and `sp` for a Silent Payments address. These keys may repeat. New bech32 formats SHOULD use their human-readable part as the key, which is why two SegWit addresses can appear as two `bc` parameters.

The address may be left out when at least one instruction is given, for a recipient who wants no on-chain fallback. Future address formats SHOULD go into parameters rather than the address, so that a wallet that only understands the address can still pay.

One rule makes this safe. A wallet may ignore any parameter it does not implement, unless the key starts with `req-`: a required key the wallet does not implement makes the whole link invalid. The hero's first wallet shows both sides. It pays a Lightning link's on-chain fallback, and it refuses a link with a `req-` key it does not know.
Some keys must not repeat. Two labels, two messages or two `pop` values make a link invalid, and BIP 321's invalid examples add two amounts.

A link may include `pop`, a percent-encoded URI prefix. After paying, a wallet that supports it decodes the prefix, appends the key it paid with (`onchain` for the address), an equals sign and the payment information, and opens the result. The payment information is the transaction in hex, or the payment preimage of a Lightning invoice.

blocks.title: Proof of payment
blocks.caption: BIP 321's four proof-of-payment examples. The model builds both published callbacks, and follows the rules for the two that point at a web page.

blocks.text: A wallet MUST NOT open a callback that would open a web browser, such as an `https` one. The author's reason is privacy: the callback should only switch back to the local app that started the payment, without revealing the sender's IP address to the recipient. If such a callback was required with `req-pop`, the wallet MUST NOT pay at all.

A link with an on-chain address is a one-time payment instruction, not a way to share contact details, since an address should not be reused. A link that carries only reusable instructions, such as a BOLT 12 offer or a Silent Payments address, MAY be reused.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: The example links use deliberately invalid addresses and invoices, as BIP 321 notes. Never treat them as payment requests.

BIP 21's grammar required a base58 address and treated parameter keys as case-sensitive. Compared with it, BIP 321 adds standard keys for other payment instructions, makes keys case-insensitive, allows bech32 and bech32m addresses and an empty address, and adds proof of payment.
BIP 21 (Nils Schneider and Matt Corallo) was assigned in 2012 and is recorded as Closed. BIP 321 (Matt Corallo) was assigned in 2024 and is recorded as Complete.
